"'''It's Too Late'''" is a song from [[Carole King]]'s second studio album, ''[[Tapestry (Carole King album)|Tapestry]]'' (1971). [[Toni Stern]] wrote the lyrics and King wrote the music. It was released as a single in April 1971 by [[Ode Records]] and reached No. 1 on the US [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] and [[Adult Contemporary (chart)|Adult Contemporary]] charts. Sales were later [[RIAA certification|platinum]]-certified by the [[Recording Industry Association of America]] (RIAA).<ref name="RIAA"/> ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' ranked "It's Too Late" and its fellow [[A-side and B-side|A-side]], "[[I Feel the Earth Move]]", as the [[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1971|No. 3 record for 1971]].

"It's Too Late" is a song from Carole King's second studio album, Tapestry (1971). Toni Stern wrote the lyrics and King wrote the music. It was released as a single in April 1971 by Ode Records and reached No. 1 on the US Billboard Hot 100 and Adult Contemporary charts. Sales were later platinum-certified by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA). Billboard ranked "It's Too Late" and its fellow A-side, "I Feel the Earth Move", as the No. 3 record for 1971.

sections.wikitext:
The lyrics describe the blameless end of a loving relationship.<ref name=words>{{cite book|title=The Words and Music of Carole King|author=Perone, J.E.|pages=34–35|year=2006|publisher=Greenwood Publishing|isbn= 9780275990275}}</ref> Music critic [[Dave Marsh]] saw implicit [[feminism]] because the woman leaves the man.<ref name=heart>{{cite book|title=The Heart of Rock and Soul|author=Marsh, D.|author-link=Dave Marsh|pages=312–313|year=1999|publisher=Da Capo Press|isbn=9780306809019}}</ref> Marsh also remarked on the maturity of the theme.<ref name=heart/>  Music critic [[Robert King|url=http://www.robertchristgau.com/get_artist.php?name=Carole+King|publisher=robertchristgau.com|author=Christgau, R.|author-link=Robert Christgau|access-date=2014-04-15}}</ref>  Marsh described Carole King's "warm, earnest singing" on the song brought out the song's sadness.<ref>{{cite web|title=500 Greatest Albums of All Time: Tapestry|date=31 May 2009|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/lists/500-greatest-albums-of-all-time-20120531/carole-king-tapestry-20120524|publisher=[[Rolling According to author James Perone, the feel of the song is enhanced by the instrumental work of [[Danny Kortchmar]] on guitar, [[Curtis Amy]] on [[saxophone]] and King on piano.<ref name=words/> Kortchmar and Amy each have an instrumental solo.<ref name=words/> ''[[Cash Box]]'' described the song as "a sensitive ballad with a strong [[Rock music|rock]] under-beat."<ref>{{cite news|title=CashBox Record Reviews|date=May 1, 1971|page=24|accessdate=2021-12-10|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/70s/1971/Cash-Box-1971-05-01.pdf|newspaper=Cash Box}}</ref> ''[[Record World]]'' said that it is "quality contemporary [[Pop music|pop]]."<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Picks of the Week|magazine=Record World|date=May 1, 1971|page=1|accessdate=2023-04-22|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Record-World/70s/71/RW-1971-05-01.pdf}}</ref>

Lyricist [[Toni Stern]] told author Sheila Weller that she wrote the lyrics in a single day, after her relationship with [[James Taylor]] ended.<ref name=SULLIVAN>{{cite book|title=Encyclopedia of Great Popular Song Recordings, volume 2 |author=Steve Sullivan |pages=326–327 |year=2013|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0810882959}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Girls Like Us: Carole King, Joni Mitchell, Carly Simon - and the Journey of a Generation |author=Sheila Weller |pages=325–328 |year=2009|publisher=Washington Square Press|isbn=9780743491488}}</ref> (This runs counter to multiple obituaries, including [[one]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/02/01/arts/music/toni-stern-dead.html?unlocked_article_code=1.QE8.j5yy.dafEyCIaJYNs&smid=nytcore-android-share | title=Toni Stern, Who Wrote Songs with Carole King, Dies at 79 | work=The New York Times | date=February 2024 | last1=Williams | first1=Alex }}</ref> by her husband of many years until her death, Jerry Rounds.) The recording won a [[Grammy Award for Record of the Year]] at the [[14th Annual Grammy Awards]] in 1972, and the song is included in [[Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time|''Rolling Stone''<nowiki/>'s 500 Greatest Songs of All Time]]. In 2003 the song was inducted into the [[Grammy Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://grammy.com/awards/hall-of-fame-award|title=GRAMMY Hall Of Fame | Hall of Fame Artists | GRAMMY.com|website=grammy.com}}</ref>
sections.text:
The lyrics describe the blameless end of a loving relationship. Music critic Dave Marsh saw implicit feminism because the woman leaves the man. Marsh also remarked on the maturity of the theme.  Music critic Robert Christgau wrote that "if there's a truer song about breaking up than 'It's Too Late,' the world (or at least AM radio) isn't ready for it."  Marsh described the melody as Tin Pan Alley and the arrangement as a cross between light jazz and "L.A. studio craftsmanship." Rolling Stone remarked that Carole King's "warm, earnest singing" on the song brought out the song's sadness. According to author James Perone, the feel of the song is enhanced by the instrumental work of Danny Kortchmar on guitar, Curtis Amy on saxophone and King on piano. Kortchmar and Amy each have an instrumental solo. Cash Box described the song as "a sensitive ballad with a strong rock under-beat." Record World said that it is "quality contemporary pop."

Lyricist Toni Stern told author Sheila Weller that she wrote the lyrics in a single day, after her relationship with James Taylor ended. (This runs counter to multiple obituaries, including one by her husband of many years until her death, Jerry Rounds.) The recording won a Grammy Award for Record of the Year at the 14th Annual Grammy Awards in 1972, and the song is included in Rolling Stone<nowiki/>'s 500 Greatest Songs of All Time. In 2003 the song was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.

sections.heading: Awards and recognition
sections.wikitext:
* King's version of "It's Too Late" peaked at No. 1 on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] and [[Adult Contemporary (chart)|Adult Contemporary]] charts. It was on the Hot 100 as a [[double A-side]] with "[[I Feel the Earth Move (Carole King song)|I Feel the Earth Move]]".
* King's version of "It's Too Late" was gold-certified by the [[Recording Industry Association of America|RIAA]].
* "It's Too Late" won a [[Grammy Award]] for Record of the Year in 1972.
* "It's Too Late" is ranked No. 469 on ''Rolling Stone''<nowiki/>'s list of the 500 greatest songs of all time. It was dropped in the 2010 version but updated to No. 310 in the 2021 version.
* Together with its other A-side, it was named by the RIAA as No. 213 of 365 [[Songs of the Century]].

British [[Electronic dance music|dance music]] production duo [[Quartz (duo)|Quartz]] ([[Ronnie Herel]] and Dave Rawlings) released their version of "It's Too Late" in 1991 on their album ''Perfect Timing'', introducing British singer-songwriter [[Dina Carroll]]. The single, released by [[Mercury Records]], earned Carroll her first hit, reaching number eight on the [[UK Singles Chart]] and on the ''[[Music Week]]'' Dance Singles chart.<ref name="UKsingles">{{cite web|url=https://www.officialcharts.com/search/singles/It%27s%20Too%20Late%20ft%20Dina%20Carroll |title=Quartz - It's Too Late ft Dina Carroll |publisher=[[Official Charts Company]] |access-date=17 October 2011 }}</ref><ref name="UKdance">{{cite magazine|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1991/MW-1991-03-23.pdf|title=Top 60 Dance Singles|magazine=[[Music Week]]|date=23 March 1991|page=26|access-date=6 April 2023}}</ref> It was also a top-5 hit in Israel and Luxembourg and a top-30 hit in Austria, peaking at number 21.

British dance music production duo Quartz (Ronnie Herel and Dave Rawlings) released their version of "It's Too Late" in 1991 on their album Perfect Timing, introducing British singer-songwriter Dina Carroll. The single, released by Mercury Records, earned Carroll her first hit, reaching number eight on the UK Singles Chart and on the Music Week Dance Singles chart. It was also a top-5 hit in Israel and Luxembourg and a top-30 hit in Austria, peaking at number 21.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext: [[James Hamilton (DJ and journalist)|James Hamilton]] from ''[[Music Week]]'' described the cover as a "gentle Carole King revival" in his weekly Dance column.<ref>{{cite magazine|first=James|last=Hamilton|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1991/MW-1991-01-26.pdf|title=Dance|magazine=[[Music Week]]|date=26 January 1991|page=16|access-date=6 April 2023|author-link=James Hamilton (DJ and journalist)}}</ref> Anthony James from ''[[New Musical Express|NME]]'' wrote, "'It's Too Late' should see a reversal in their fortunes. Featuring the gutsy vocals of Dina Carroll it's a truly kickin' track but with a commercial edge. Carole King will turn in her rave."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=James|last=Anthony|url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/nothingelseon/52294831216/|title=Quartz 'A' All|magazine=[[New Musical Express|NME]]|date=16 February 1991|page=24|access-date=6 April 2023}}</ref> Another ''NME'' editor, Ian McCann, complimented it as "a genuine hit".<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Ian|last=McCann|url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/nothingelseon/52409111076/|title=Short Circuit|magazine=[[New Musical Express|NME]]|date=27 July 1991|page=30|access-date=29 April 2023}}</ref>

thumb|upright|Gloria Estefan, 2001

Cuban American singer and songwriter Gloria Estefan released her cover of "It's Too Late" in 1995 as the third promotional single (in the US), and fourth overall single released from her fourth studio album, Hold Me, Thrill Me, Kiss Me (1994). It was produced by Emilio Estefan, Jr., Jorge Casas and Clay Ostwald, and released in May 1995 by Epic Records.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext: [[AllMusic]] editor Eddie Huffman described Estefan's version as "[a] moment of genuine pathos" in his review of the ''Hold Me, Thrill Me, Kiss Me'' album.<ref>{{cite web|first=Eddie|last=Huffman|url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/hold-me-thrill-me-kiss-me-mw0000626621|title=Gloria Estefan - Hold Me, Thrill Me, Kiss Me|publisher=[[AllMusic]]|access-date=2020-02-24}}</ref> Steve Baltin from ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]'' magazine felt the singer "does a decent job with the vocals, but this is one of those songs that everybody feels they own. As such, it’s better off being left alone."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Steve|last=Baltin|title=Pop Singles|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/90s/1995/CB-1995-06-17.pdf|magazine=[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]|date=1995-06-17|page=7|accessdate=2022-11-07}}</ref> Chuck Campbell from ''[[Knoxville News Sentinel]]'' viewed it as a "faithful" remake of Carole King's 1971 hit, "though [[Tim Mitchell]]'s intrusive electric-guitar solo is an unwelcome addition."<ref>Campbell, Chuck (1994-10-28). "Bedtime' With Madonna Is A Bit Drowsy". ''[[Knoxville News Sentinel]]''.</ref> Phil Shanklin of ReviewsRevues remarked that King's voice does possess the same warmth as Estefan's.<ref>{{cite web |first= Phil |last= Shanklin |title= 100 Essential CDs – Number 72 –Hold Me, Thrill Me, Kiss Me –Gloria Estefan |url= https://reviewsrevues.com/2015/11/22/100-essential-cds-number-72-hold-me-thrill-me-kiss-me-gloria-estefan/ |website= Reviewsrevues.com |date= 2015-11-22 |access-date= 2020-10-14 |archive-date= 2020-10-24 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20201024055607/https://reviewsrevues.com/2015/11/22/100-essential-cds-number-72-hold-me-thrill-me-kiss-me-gloria-estefan/ |url-status= dead }}</ref> Tony Cross from ''[[Smash Hits]]'' gave Estefan's version two out of five, writing that "Glo's done a fine job tweeking it into shape by funking it up a bit."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Tony|last=Cross|url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/57779449@N02/54314380255/in/album-72177720323683892|title=Singles|magazine=[[Smash Hits]]|date=1995-05-24|page=58|access-date=2025-02-10}}</ref>
sections.text: AllMusic editor Eddie Huffman described Estefan's version as "[a] moment of genuine pathos" in his review of the Hold Me, Thrill Me, Kiss Me album. Steve Baltin from Cash Box magazine felt the singer "does a decent job with the vocals, but this is one of those songs that everybody feels they own. As such, it’s better off being left alone." Chuck Campbell from Knoxville News Sentinel viewed it as a "faithful" remake of Carole King's 1971 hit, "though Tim Mitchell's intrusive electric-guitar solo is an unwelcome addition." Phil Shanklin of ReviewsRevues remarked that King's voice does possess the same warmth as Estefan's. Tony Cross from Smash Hits gave Estefan's version two out of five, writing that "Glo's done a fine job tweeking it into shape by funking it up a bit."

* 1973: [[Mike James Kirkland]] on the album ''Doin' it Right''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/doin-it-right-mw0000602166#trackListing|title=Doin' It Right - Mike James Kirkland | Album | AllMusic|via=www.allmusic.com}}</ref>
